sources.shortCitation: “At the Beachcomber on opening night” — Desert Sun
sources.fullCitation: “At the Beachcomber on opening night was Hoagy Carmichael, center. Here he is chatting with a fellow songwriter Sidney Clare, left, and Arthur Gordon, of Fleishman Distilleries.” Photograph. Desert Sun (Palm Springs, Calif.), vol. 30, no. 38, 13 October 1956, p. 6. California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside.
sources.title: At the Beachcomber on opening night
sources.creator: Desert Sun (photograph credit)
sources.repository: California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside
sources.researchNote: The caption identifies Sidney Clare as “a fellow songwriter” beside Hoagy Carmichael, distinguishing him from namesakes. The photograph documents Clare in Palm Springs later in life; the occasion is the opening of the Beachcomber, not a professional gathering.

sources.shortCitation: “Song Writers to Perform” — Santa Ana Journal
sources.fullCitation: “Song Writers to Perform: Lew Pollack and Sidney Mitchell, authors of song hits, who will be among the featured artists at the President’s Ball. The ball opens at 8:45 tonight at the Valencia Ball Room and the proceeds will be devoted to the fight against infantile paralysis.” Photograph with caption. Santa Ana Journal (Santa Ana, Calif.), vol. 3, no. 231, 27 January 1938, p. 7. California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside.
sources.title: Song Writers to Perform
sources.creator: Photographer unidentified
sources.repository: California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside
sources.researchNote: The two men appear as working songwriters scheduled to perform at a President’s Birthday Ball benefiting the campaign against infantile paralysis. The caption names Lew Pollack and Sidney Mitchell but does not distinguish which man is which; the image therefore documents the pair rather than serving as an individually identified portrait.

sources.shortCitation: “Harry Richman sings love songs in earnest now” — Madera Daily Tribune
sources.fullCitation: “Harry Richman sings love songs in earnest now.” With a photograph of Richman and Clara Bow. Madera Daily Tribune and Madera Mercury (Madera, Calif.), vol. 44, no. 84, 8 August 1929, p. 4. California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside.
sources.title: Harry Richman sings love songs in earnest now
sources.creator: Photographer unidentified
sources.repository: California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside
sources.publication: Madera Daily Tribune and Madera Mercury
sources.researchNote: The notice describes Harry Richman as a star of the Scandals, a Brunswick recording artist who had recently recorded “Now I’m in Love” and “My Dear” in Los Angeles, a singer active on stage, on records and in nightclubs, and a performer under contract to United Artists for a film then titled The Song of Broadway. The accompanying paragraph also reports his engagement to Clara Bow.

sources.shortCitation: “It pays to be wacky” — Santa Ana Journal
sources.fullCitation: “It pays to be wacky, so — ‘The fly outflew the flea’.” Chicago dispatch, with a photograph captioned “‘The lyric is lousy’ — so said Terry Shand, left. But neither Larry Shay, center, who helped Shand write the music, nor Jimmie Eaton, right, who wrote the words to ‘The fly outflew the flea’ care so long as the public likes the song.” Santa Ana Journal (Santa Ana, Calif.), vol. 3, no. 60, 9 July 1937, p. 18. California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside.
sources.title: It pays to be wacky, so — “The fly outflew the flea”
sources.creator: Photographer unidentified
sources.repository: California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside
sources.researchNote: The caption places Shay in the middle of the three men and states his part in the song: he helped Terry Shand write the music to a lyric by Jimmie Eaton. The interview quotes him on how the piece came about — “Jimmie wrote the lyric and Terry and I fitted in the music. It has catchy tempo and words and that is all you need” — and an unnamed publisher sets out what launching a song then cost: three or four thousand dollars for printing, artwork and orchestration, and sixty to two hundred and fifty dollars a week for the men who placed it with radio singers. The dispatch is datelined Chicago and was carried by a wire service, so the same text and picture appeared in other papers.

sources.title: News item on Champagne Lady
sources.fullCitation: [News item on “Champagne Lady,” dedicated to Evelyn Laye]. Daily News (Los Angeles), 8 December 1934, p. 15. California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside.
sources.repository: California Digital Newspaper Collection, Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research, University of California, Riverside
sources.researchNote: The contemporary item explicitly names Walter Jurmann and Bronisław Kaper as the composers and identifies Gus Kahn as the lyric writer with whom they collaborated. It presents the song as a tribute to Evelyn Laye and says that it was given to her shortly before her marriage to Frank Lawton. The reference to The Night Is Young describes Laye’s work at the time and does not establish that “Champagne Lady” was used in the film. No published score, copyright registration or recording of the song has yet been identified.
